claim: GPS tracking data (1 Hz) were collected from 25 wild olive baboons (Papio anubis) belonging to a single troop at Mpala Research Centre in Laikipia, Kenya, from 1 August - 2 September, 2012.
source: GPS tracking data (1 Hz) were collected from 25 wild olive baboons (Papio anubis) belonging to a single troop at Mpala Research Centre in Laikipia, Kenya, from 1 August - 2 September, 2012.
evidence: Direct statement in the Materials and methods section describing the data collection parameters.

claim: Tracked individuals included 81% (23/29) of the adult and subadult members of the troop, as well as two juveniles (for a total of 25).
source: Tracked individuals included 81% (23/ 29) of the adult and subadult members of the troop, as well as two juveniles (for a total of 25).
evidence: Direct statement describing the sample composition.

claim: Aerial imagery of the habitat was collected from 9–17 January, 2015 using an eBee fixed-wing UAV (Sensefly Ltd).
source: Aerial imagery of the habitat was collected from 9–17 January, 2015 using an eBee fixed-wing UAV (Sensefly Ltd).
evidence: Direct statement in the Materials and methods section describing the aerial imagery collection.

claim: The mapped area covered 3.3 km2, representing approximately 2/3 of the area covered by the baboon troop during the first 14 days.
source: The mapped area covered 3.3 km2, representing approximately 2/3 of the area covered by the baboon troop during the first 14 days (the period from which we analyzed tracking data).
evidence: Direct statement describing the extent of the mapped area.

claim: A three-dimensional reconstruction of the habitat was generated with c. 5 cm precision.
source: from these images generated a 3-dimensional reconstruction of the habitat with c. 5 cm precision (Appendix 1—figure 1; Appendix 1—figure 2; Appendix 1—figure 3; Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement describing the precision of the 3D reconstruction.

claim: Baboons' preference for locations that other troop members have recently traversed is the most important predictor of individual movement decisions.
source: A previously unexplored social influence – baboons' preference for locations that other troop members have recently traversed – is the most important predictor of individual movement decisions.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a primary finding, supported by multi-model inference results showing recently used space as the top-ranked feature.

claim: The best supported time scale for the recently used space effect is approximately 4.5 minutes.
source: The best supported time scale associated with this effect is approximately 4.5 min (Appendix 1—figure 8); in other words, baboons show a preference to move to locations that have been occupied by many of their troop-mates within that timescale.
evidence: Direct statement based on maximum likelihood analysis of temporal scales.

claim: Both social factors and habitat factors are important in determining baboon movement decisions.
source: Our analysis indicates that both social factors and habitat factors are important in determining baboon movement decisions.
evidence: Stated as a result based on model comparison showing increased predictive power when both types of features are included.

claim: Models incorporating both social and habitat features have greater predictive power than models incorporating only one or the other.
source: Comparing the predictive ability of models incorporating only social features (social only), only habitat features (habitat only), all features (habitat + social), or no features (null model) shows a clear increase in predictive power for models including both social and habitat features, as compared to those incorporating only one or the other (Figure 1B).
evidence: Direct statement supported by Figure 1B showing predictive accuracy comparisons.

claim: Baboons tend to move away from the sleep site in the morning and towards it in the evening.
source: The direction relative to the location of the sleep site emerges as an important predictor of individual movement decisions (sleep site dir feature ranked second, Figure 1C), with baboons tending to move away from the sleep site in the morning and towards it in the evening.
evidence: Direct statement based on model fitting results and feature ranking.

claim: Baboons show a strong preference to follow roads once on them.
source: Whether a location is on a road influences its probability of being selected (roads feature, Figure 1C), and in particular, baboons show a strong preference to follow roads once on them (Appendix 1—figures 10–11).
evidence: Direct statement based on model results and supported by referenced figures.

claim: Smaller game paths have a less pronounced influence on baboon movement decisions than man-made roads.
source: By contrast, smaller game paths (Appendix 1—figure 3), although much more numerous than man-made roads, have a less pronounced influence on baboon movement decisions (paths feature is low-ranked, Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct statement based on feature ranking comparison.

claim: Baboons tend to avoid locations of high vegetation density over a local scale of 2.5 m.
source: Over a similarly local scale (2.5 m, Appendix 1—figure 6), baboons tend to avoid locations of high vegetation density (env density feature, Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct statement based on model results at a specific spatial scale.

claim: Baboons incorporate a variety of both habitat and social elements operating over a range of spatial scales when making movement decisions.
source: Thus, our model-fitting results support that baboons incorporate a variety of both habitat and social elements operating over a range of spatial scales when making movement decisions.
evidence: Summary statement based on the multi-model inference results.

claim: The true location selected by a baboon is likely to be the one that more of its troop-mates have recently passed through.
source: The result is a sigmoidal response (Figure 3A), where the true location selected by a baboon is likely to be the one that more of its troop-mates have recently passed through, with this probability increasing as the difference in the number of troop-mates to occupy the two alternative locations increases.
evidence: Direct statement based on analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When a baboon starts on a road, it takes 3–4 more troop mates to walk through an off-road location before a baboon will have an equal chance of picking it compared to an on-road location.
source: For example, from Figure 3B one can determine that when a baboon starts on a road, it takes 3–4 more troop mates to walk through an off-road location before a baboon will have an equal chance of picking it compared to an on-road location (indicated by the red line crossing y = 0.5).
evidence: Direct statement based on quantitative analysis of Figure 3B.

claim: Roads and the previous locations of troop members strongly influence the locations where baboons choose to move.
source: This result suggests that both roads and the previous locations of troop members strongly influence the locations where baboons choose to move, with the relative contributions of these two influences reflected in the shape of the sigmoidal curve (Figure 3).
evidence: Direct statement based on analysis of Figure 3.

claim: In the morning baboons were more likely to choose locations farther away from the sleep site, and conversely for the evening.
source: The sleep site direction is found to introduce a similar bias (Figure 3D–F), where in the morning baboons were more likely to choose locations farther away from the sleep site, and conversely for the evening.
evidence: Direct statement based on analysis shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: The importance of roads is stronger in the morning and evening relative to the middle of the day.
source: For example, models fitted using data that correspond to different times of day demonstrate that the importance of roads is stronger in the morning and evening relative to the middle of the day.
evidence: Direct statement based on context-specific model fitting.

claim: The direction of the sleep site plays a larger role in the morning and evening than in the midday.
source: The direction of the sleep site also plays a larger role in the morning and evening than in the midday.
evidence: Direct statement based on context-specific model fitting.

claim: During morning and evening, the troop tends to be more elongated, and to move more often in a directed manner with lower tilt.
source: During morning and evening, the troop tends to be more elongated, and to move more often in a directed manner with lower tilt (Appendix 1—figure 18, Appendix 1—figure 22), all of which would be expected based on either more goal-directed movement (toward or away from the sleep site) and/or movement that utilizes roads.
evidence: Direct statement based on group-level analysis shown in referenced figures.

claim: The group spent considerably more time on roads during morning and evening than during the midday (12.1% in morning and evening vs. 7.5% during midday).
source: Indeed, the group spent considerably more time on roads during morning and evening than during the midday (12.1% in morning and evening vs. 7.5% during midday, Appendix 1—figure 23).
evidence: Direct statement with specific percentages from data analysis.

claim: Groups move faster and in a more directed manner on roads.
source: Moreover, comparing group structure on and off roads supports the idea that baboons use roads as an efficient method of travel, with groups moving faster and in a more directed manner on roads (Figure 5B, Appendix 1—figure 20).
evidence: Direct statement based on comparison of group structure in different contexts.

claim: In dense environments, baboons' movement decisions become more strongly influenced by local-scale heterogeneity in vegetation relative to other factors.
source: Although when data are considered in aggregate, environment density plays a relatively small role in influencing the local movement decisions of individual baboons (Figure 1C), its importance increases when considering individual movement decisions in particularly dense environments, surpassing both roads and social density (Appendix 1—figure 15B). Thus, in dense environments, baboons' movement decisions become more strongly influenced by local-scale heterogeneity in vegetation relative to other factors.
evidence: Direct statement based on context-specific model fitting.

claim: High-density areas are associated with lower group polarization, as well as slower troop speed and less directed travel.
source: At the group level, high-density areas are associated with lower group polarization, as well as slower troop speed and less directed travel (Figure 5C).
evidence: Direct statement based on group-level analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Vegetation structure plays an important role in constraining the degree of movement coordination in animal groups.
source: These changes suggest that vegetation structure plays an important role in constraining the degree of movement coordination in animal groups.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed changes in group coordination in different vegetation densities.

claim: The importance of animal paths at the individual level increases in areas with a particularly high density of paths.
source: Similarly, though animal paths are low ranked in feature weight when models are fitted across all data, their importance at the individual level increases in areas with a particularly high density of paths (Appendix 1—figure 15C).
evidence: Direct statement based on context-specific model fitting.

claim: Areas with a high density of paths are associated with faster, more directed, and more polarized movement at the group level.
source: Areas with a high density of paths are also associated with faster, more directed, and more polarized movement at the group level (Appendix 1—figure 17, Appendix 1—figure 21).
evidence: Direct statement based on group-level analysis.

claim: Habitat features receive larger weights across all group-level properties than does time of day.
source: Computing the feature weights of each of these predictors via multi-model inference reveals that the habitat features receive larger weights across all group-level properties than does time of day (Figure 6).
evidence: Direct statement based on multi-model inference results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Group structure is shaped more by the current habitat the baboons occupy than by the temporal context.
source: This result suggests that group structure is shaped more by the current habitat the baboons occupy than by the temporal context.
evidence: Inference drawn from the feature weight comparison.

claim: Roads and areas of high path density are associated with similar changes to group structure – i.e. groups become faster, more elongated, and more polarized.
source: The fits also reveal that roads and areas of high path density are associated with similar changes to group structure – i.e. groups become faster, more elongated, and more polarized – but that roads are generally a stronger predictor of these changes (higher feature weight, Figure 6).
evidence: Direct statement based on model fitting results.

claim: Roads are generally a stronger predictor of group structure changes than areas of high path density.
source: The fits also reveal that roads and areas of high path density are associated with similar changes to group structure – i.e. groups become faster, more elongated, and more polarized – but that roads are generally a stronger predictor of these changes (higher feature weight, Figure 6).
evidence: Direct statement based on feature weight comparison.

claim: Baboon troops range in size from a few to over a hundred individuals.
source: Baboon troops, which range in size from a few to over a hundred individuals, normally remain cohesive while foraging throughout the day, despite traveling long distances over variable routes through a heterogeneous savanna habitat (Byrne, 2000; Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Baboon troops normally remain cohesive while foraging throughout the day, despite traveling long distances over variable routes through a heterogeneous savanna habitat.
source: Baboon troops, which range in size from a few to over a hundred individuals, normally remain cohesive while foraging throughout the day, despite traveling long distances over variable routes through a heterogeneous savanna habitat (Byrne, 2000; Cheney and Seyfarth, 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Olive baboons are generalist omnivores, and typically feed on dispersed and widespread resources throughout their range.
source: Olive baboons are generalist omnivores, and typically feed on dispersed and widespread resources throughout their range.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about olive baboon ecology.

claim: The two major predators of baboons are leopards and lions.
source: The two major predators of baboons are leopards and lions (Cowlishaw, 1994).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Leopards, which will kill baboons both during the day and at night, are very common at the study site.
source: Leopards, which will kill baboons both during the day and at night, are very common at the study site.
evidence: Statement based on knowledge of the study site and leopard behavior.

claim: To avoid predation at night, baboons choose safe sleeping sites and generally return to the same site each evening.
source: To avoid predation at night, baboons choose safe sleeping sites and generally return to the same site each evening (although we observed our study troop temporarily changing sleeping site after the end of the study period after a leopard was observed at their sleeping site the previous night).
evidence: Statement based on general baboon behavior and specific observation.

claim: Lions are much less common at the study site, and were unlikely to represent a major threat to the study group.
source: Lions are much less common at the study site, and were unlikely to represent a major threat to our study group.
evidence: Statement based on knowledge of the study site.

claim: Maintaining cohesion with conspecifics can benefit individuals by reducing predation risk, improving foraging efficiency, and, in some cases, by enhancing sensing of environmental gradients.
source: Maintaining cohesion with conspecifics can benefit individuals by reducing predation risk, improving foraging efficiency (Krause and Ruxton, 2002), and, in some cases, by enhancing sensing of environmental gradients (Berdahl et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Studies of collective motion have tended to discount the potential role of environmental complexity by either conducting experiments in relatively simple or featureless environments or by focusing only on social influences on movement.
source: Despite this, studies of collective motion have tended to discount the potential role of environmental complexity by either conducting experiments in relatively simple or featureless environments composed of mostly unobstructed space, as in many lab experiments (Buhl et al., 2006; Katz et al., 2011; Herbert-Read et al., 2011; Rosenthal et al., 2015) (but see [Berdahl et al., 2013]), or when they do consider animals moving in structured environments, by focusing only on social influences on movement (Biro et al., 2006; Strandburg-Peshkin et al., 2015; King and Sueur, 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: At the individual level, animals can exhibit goal-directed movement toward or away from certain habitat features.
source: At the individual level, animals can exhibit goal-directed movement toward or away from certain habitat features (Polansky et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Animals can be constrained by physical features of the landscape such as steep hills or dense vegetation.
source: They can also be constrained by physical features of the landscape such as steep hills or dense vegetation (Wall et al., 2006; McLean et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Theoretical models suggest that when some individuals within a collectively-moving group exhibit goal-directed movement, an elongated group structure can emerge.
source: For example, theoretical models suggest that when some individuals within a collectively-moving group exhibit goal-directed movement, an elongated group structure can emerge (Couzin et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Habitat factors such as vegetation density could constrain the extent to which animals can coordinate their movement, both by limiting the flow of information and by imposing physical constraints on where and how fast animals can move.
source: Habitat factors such as vegetation density could constrain the extent to which animals can coordinate their movement, both by limiting the flow of information (e.g. by reducing visibility to other group members) and by imposing physical constraints on where and how fast animals can move.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential mechanisms.

claim: Both individual movement rules and emergent group structure could be altered by environmental context, leading groups to be observed in different states or exhibit different behaviors depending on the area of their home range they occupy on a moment-to-moment basis.
source: Moreover, both individual movement rules and emergent group structure could be altered by environmental context, leading groups to be observed in different states or exhibit different behaviors depending on the area of their home range they occupy on a moment-to-moment basis.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential effects.

claim: To understand how the varied patterns of group spatial organization and movement dynamics seen in nature emerge, taking the habitat into account is likely to be of critical importance.
source: Thus, to understand how the varied patterns of group spatial organization and movement dynamics seen in nature emerge, taking the habitat into account is likely to be of critical importance.
evidence: Inference drawn from the discussion of habitat influences.

claim: Advances in GPS tracking capabilities now make it possible to collect data at a high enough spatial and temporal resolution that fine-scale movement decisions and social interactions can be resolved.
source: Advances in GPS tracking capabilities now make it possible to collect data at a high enough spatial and temporal resolution that fine-scale movement decisions and social interactions can be resolved (Nagy et al., 2010; King et al., 2012; Mann et al., 2014; Giuggioli et al., 2015; Strandburg-Peshkin et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The increased consumer availability of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), coupled with computational advances in image stitching and three-dimensional landscape reconstruction, have made these tools increasingly accessible to researchers in biology.
source: At the same time, the increased consumer availability of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), coupled with computational advances in image stitching and three-dimensional landscape reconstruction, have made these tools increasingly accessible to researchers in biology (Anderson and Gaston, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Baboons often travelled 5–6 kms per day during the study period.
source: In fact, baboons in our troop often travelled 5–6 kms per day during the study period, probably because conditions were dry and food, although not scarce, was not abundant enough close to their sleep site to sustain the entire troop.
evidence: Direct statement based on observation during the study.

claim: Conditions were dry during the study period and food, although not scarce, was not abundant enough close to the sleep site to sustain the entire troop.
source: In fact, baboons in our troop often travelled 5–6 kms per day during the study period, probably because conditions were dry and food, although not scarce, was not abundant enough close to their sleep site to sustain the entire troop.
evidence: Statement based on observation and inference about environmental conditions.

claim: The study troop forages on mixed resources that are widely distributed (e.g. grass roots and prickly pear fruit).
source: Our observation in the field is that the troop forages on mixed resources that are widely distributed (e.g. grass roots and prickly pear fruit), meaning that this explanation seems unlikely.
evidence: Direct statement based on field observations.

claim: The importance of following others could reflect a risk reduction strategy, since locations that conspecifics have recently passed through have already been effectively 'pre-screened' for threats such as leopards or venomous snakes.
source: Alternatively, the importance of following others could reflect a risk reduction strategy, since locations that conspecifics have recently passed through have already been effectively 'pre-screened' for threats such as leopards or venomous snakes.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed behavior.

claim: The decrease in the importance rank of the recently used feature when the troop is in open habitats supports the hypothesis that following others provides anti-predator benefits.
source: This hypothesis is supported by the decrease in the importance rank of the recently used feature when the troop is in open habitats (Appendix 1—figure 15B), as there are likely to be fewer anti-predator benefits to be gained by following others in open areas.
evidence: Inference drawn from context-specific model results.

claim: Following in the footsteps of others is a less cognitively demanding task than carving out one's own path.
source: A final possibility is that since following in the footsteps of others is a less cognitively demanding task than carving out one's own path (Piyapong et al., 2007), by generally following these paths baboons are reducing the cognitive effort of navigation (Kool et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Baboons' tendency to follow in the footsteps of others is likely to have consequences for the aggregate space use patterns of baboon troops, with troops making use of a smaller portion of the area within their surroundings than would be naively expected if individuals were moving more randomly within the troop's boundaries.
source: Regardless of the explanation, baboons' tendency to follow in the footsteps of others is likely to have consequences for the aggregate space use patterns of baboon troops, with troops making use of a smaller portion of the area within their surroundings than would be naively expected if individuals were moving more randomly within the troop's boundaries, which in turn could alter their impact on the environment around them.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed behavior.

claim: Where individuals position themselves within groups is thought to reflect a trade-off between forging new ground to find resources and being exposed to predators.
source: Where individuals position themselves within groups is thought to reflect a trade-off between forging new ground to find resources and being exposed to predators (Hirsch, 2007; Krause, 1994; Parrish and Edelstein-Keshet, 1999; Hirsch, 2011; Teichroeb et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The extent to which animals follow in each others footsteps will have an important impact on the rate at which individuals are exposed to new areas - and hence the rate at which they will encounter both new resources and stationary predators.
source: While work in this area has typically focused on how this tradeoff can drive differences in the amount of time individuals spend at the front vs back of the group, or in the center vs periphery, our results suggest that the extent to which animals follow in each others footsteps is another dynamic which should be considered, as this factor will have an important impact on the rate at which individuals are exposed to new areas - and hence the rate at which they will encounter both new resources and stationary predators.
evidence: Inference drawn from the study results.

claim: Roads may facilitate animal movement, perhaps by serving as navigational landmarks.
source: The importance of roads is consistent with studies in other species which suggest that roads may facilitate animal movement (Dickson et al., 2005), perhaps by serving as navigational landmarks (Mann et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The weaker influence of paths compared to roads is consistent with the hypothesis that roads serve as navigational landmarks, as the abundance and tortuosity of paths could make them less useful as navigational aids.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the weaker influence of paths in our analysis (Figure 1C), whose sheer abundance and tortuosity could make them less useful as navigational aids.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of road and path effects.

claim: The temporal difference in road importance is likely to reflect the needs of the troop to travel away from their core zone (near their sleeping site) to forage.
source: This temporal difference is likely to reflect the needs of the troop to travel away from their core zone (near their sleeping site) to forage (Appendix 1—figure 23).
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed temporal patterns.

claim: Changes in coordination and group spatial organization as a function of environmental factors will have important consequences for understanding both the mechanistic basis of group coordination and its costs and benefits.
source: Changes in coordination and group spatial organization as a function of environmental factors will have important consequences for understanding both the mechanistic basis of group coordination and its costs and benefits.
evidence: Inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: Habitat influences extend beyond the level of individual decisions to the collective dynamics of the group, leading to changes in emergent group structure and coordination in different environmental contexts.
source: Moreover, habitat influences extend beyond the level of individual decisions to the collective dynamics of the group, leading to changes in emergent group structure and coordination in different environmental contexts.
evidence: Summary statement based on the group-level analysis results.

claim: Changes in group structure could reflect direct habitat constraints on movement (such as physical barriers to movement), but also behavioral changes associated with different habitats (such as a shift from foraging to directed travel in different environments).
source: This effect is manifested in our dataset in the fast movement and elongated group structures formed on roads and areas of high path density, and the decrease in coordination when moving through dense habitats. These changes could reflect direct habitat constraints on movement (such as physical barriers to movement), but also behavioral changes associated with different habitats (such as a shift from foraging to directed travel in different environments).
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed patterns.

claim: Roads and sleeping sites are relatively dramatic features of the habitat that have a large impact on baboon movement patterns.
source: Our results suggest that, although few in number and in total area, roads and sleeping sites are relatively dramatic features of the habitat that have a large impact on baboon movement patterns.
evidence: Summary inference from the results.

claim: As the resolution at which we can map both the movements of animals and their environments improve, the integration of habitat features into studies of collective behavior - and conversely the incorporation of within-group social interactions into studies in movement ecology - will be critical for understanding the movement patterns of social animals.
source: As the resolution at which we can map both the movements of animals and their environments improve, the integration of habitat features into studies of collective behavior - and conversely the incorporation of within-group social interactions into studies in movement ecology - will be critical for understanding the movement patterns of social animals.
evidence: Inference about future research directions based on the study's findings.

claim: The methods employed and many of the insights gained are likely to extend to a variety of social animals.
source: While the results shown here are specific to the system we explore, the methods employed and many of the insights gained are likely to extend to a variety of social animals.
evidence: Inference about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: Step selection is a widely employed framework for assessing the environmental drivers of animal movement patterns.
source: Step selection is a widely employed framework for assessing the environmental drivers of animal movement patterns (Thurfjell et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Step selection models have previously been employed to infer the habitat preferences of animals, as well as their responses to distributions of predators and competitors.
source: Step selection models have previously been employed to infer the habitat preferences of animals (Fortin et al., 2005; Coulon et al., 2008; Hodson et al., 2010), as well as their responses to distributions of predators (Fortin et al., 2005; Basille et al., 2015; Latombe et al., 2014), and competitors (Vanak et al., 2013; Potts et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Step selection models have not before been applied to the study of the fine-scale social interactions within animal groups and their interplay with nonsocial influences on movement.
source: However, to our knowledge step selection models have not before been applied to the study of the fine-scale social interactions within animal groups and their interplay with nonsocial influences on movement.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the approach.

claim: Images were automatically combined using Postflight Terra 3D software (Pix4D) to reconstruct a three-dimensional point cloud image of the landscape.
source: After collection, images were automatically combined using Postflight Terra 3D software (Pix4D) to reconstruct a three-dimensional point cloud image of the landscape, and these were used to identify all habitat features.
evidence: Direct statement describing the image processing method.

claim: All procedures were subject to ethical review and were carried out in accordance with the approved guidelines set out by the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation of the Republic of Kenya (NACOSTI/P/15/5727/4608).
source: All procedures were subject to ethical review and were carried out in accordance with the approved guidelines set out by the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation of the Republic of Kenya (NACOSTI/P/15/5727/4608).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Baboon tracking was approved by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (IACUC 2012.0601.2015).
source: Baboon tracking was approved by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (IACUC 2012.0601.2015).
evidence: Direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Baboons are effectively 'commuting' to and from foraging locations during the start and end of each day.
source: This suggests that baboons are effectively 'commuting' to and from foraging locations during the start and end of each day (Appendix 1—figure 15A).
evidence: Inference drawn from the temporal patterns in movement behavior.

claim: The preference for recently-used locations is shown to be for a particular location in space rather than a general direction of travel.
source: This result is consistent with the previously-observed preference of baboons to follow the majority of troop-mates (Strandburg-Peshkin et al., 2015), but in this case the preference is shown to be for a particular location in space rather than a general direction of travel.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison with prior findings.

claim: As baboons move through space they effectively 'pave the way' for their troop mates, who tend to follow in the footsteps of larger subgroups.
source: Thus as baboons move through space they effectively 'pave the way' for their troop mates, who tend to follow in the footsteps of larger subgroups.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observed preference for recently-used locations.

claim: Both the data collection periods (August-September 2012 for GPS tracking and January 2015 for aerial imagery) had similar ecological conditions (dry season) and habitat characteristics (trees, roads, bushes) were unlikely to have changed much over this period.
source: Although we had a gap between the two data collection periods, both had similar ecological conditions (dry season) and habitat characteristics (trees, roads, bushes) were unlikely to have changed much over this period.
evidence: Statement about the comparability of data collection periods.
